newsitem.title: USA: Clinton picks Tenet as CIA nominee.
newsitem.headline: Clinton picks Tenet as CIA nominee.

text.p: President Bill Clinton has decided to nominate acting CIA Director George Tenet to be permanent chief of the spy agency and director of the whole U.S. intelligence community, senior administration officials said on Wednesday.
"The president believes he (Tenet) is well qualified for the post," said one senior White House official. "He's more than satisfied."

The nomination of Tenet, 44, who was deputy CIA director before his interim appointment as acting director last December, replaces that of Anthony Lake, who withrew from consideration on Monday after harsh Senate confirmation hearings.
Tenet, a close friend of Lake's, was unlikely to encounter similar stiff opposition in winning Senate confirmation.
He has served as staff director of the Senate Intelligence Committee, which anchors the confirmation process, and he underwent scrutiny when confirmed by the Senate as deputy CIA director.
Administration officials said Clinton was likely to make the formal announcement before he departed on Wednesday night for a summit in Helsinki with Russian President Boris Yeltsin.
Among other previous key posts in Washington, Tenet also worked at the White House from 1993 until 1995 as chief intelligence adviser to Lake, who was Clinton's national security adviser.
He crafted presidential directives on intelligence priorities, security coordination, spy-catching and satellite remote-sensing policies.
His Capitol Hill experience came as staff director on the Senate Intelligence Committee from 1988-93.
Lake abruptly ended his own quest for confirmation as CIA director on Monday, After a combative three-month process that he said was more than he could bear.

Lake said he feared the agency and his own integrity would be damaged by the prolonged pounding from Republican senators on issues ranging from his knowledge of questionable White House fund-raising practices to his management of the National Security Council staff, his failure to divest himself of some stock and his role in U.S. policy in Bosnia.

Critics led by Senate Intelligence Committee Richard Shelby, an Alabama Republican, said they were pursuing legitimate lines of inquiry as to whether Lake was competent to manage the gigantic, sprawling U.S. intelligence community.
Its components, the CIA and 12 sister spy agencies, employ about 80,000 people, according to Shelby, and currently spend an aggregate of about $30 billion a year.
